strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation: noisy multi-view object captions caused by occlusion, viewpoint bias, and imperfect aggregation. This is well motivated for embodied AI and robotics settings.

The proposed pipeline combines several sensible components: dynamic object-dependent downsampling, re-shot view rendering from object point clouds, uncertainty estimation by comparing crop and re-shot captions, and context-based refinement for uncertain objects. The system-level framing is coherent and easy to follow.

Empirical results on Replica show consistent improvements over ConceptGraphs variants in human-evaluated node precision and edge precision, with notably higher valid object/edge counts and fewer duplicates. The ablations also support the importance of re-shot uncertainty estimation and the RAG-style refinement.

The paper includes implementation details, pseudocode, qualitative examples, an ethics statement, and a reproducibility statement, which improves clarity and makes the intended pipeline relatively understandable.
weaknesses: The evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. All experiments are on Replica, a synthetic indoor dataset, with no evaluation on real RGB-D sequences, ScanNet/3RScan-style data, or downstream robotics tasks. This makes it hard to assess robustness under the real-world conditions used to motivate the work.

The human evaluation protocol is under-specified. The manuscript does not clearly report the number of annotators, number of evaluated samples, inter-annotator agreement, statistical significance, or whether comparisons were blind to method identity. Since the main node/edge precision claims rely on human judgments, this is a significant weakness.

The method depends heavily on black-box commercial models, especially GPT-4/GPT-4o-mini, but prompts and non-critical hyperparameters are deferred to a future code release. This weakens reproducibility, and the results may be sensitive to model versions, API changes, and prompt details.

The novelty is incremental at the algorithmic level. Much of the pipeline builds directly on ConceptGraphs, while the main additions are heuristic re-rendering, caption agreement filtering, nearest-object contextual prompting, and dynamic voxel sizing. These are useful engineering ideas, but the paper does not provide a deep technical analysis showing why they should generalize.

The term RAG is somewhat overstated: retrieval appears to be position-based nearest-neighbor retrieval of a nearby low-uncertainty object caption, not a richer learned or semantic retrieval system. The paper does not compare against stronger contextual prompting/retrieval alternatives beyond random retrieval.

Efficiency claims are incomplete. The reported speedup focuses on object mapping time for one setting, but the full pipeline adds re-shot rendering, VLM captioning, LLM aggregation, and refinement. There is no end-to-end runtime/cost analysis, which is important for a method motivated partly by speed.

The dynamic downsampling formulation is heuristic and not deeply justified. The voxel size scales with the square root of bounding-box diagonal length, which has unclear dimensional interpretation, and the paper does not provide sensitivity analysis for this design or for alpha/beta, top-k, top-50% uncertainty split, or retrieval choices.

Evaluation of semantic segmentation and ablation uses GPT-4o as a semantic assigner, introducing possible evaluator bias and making results difficult to reproduce. The segmentation table also shows the proposed method is comparable but not clearly superior to strong baselines such as OpenMask3D in f-mIoU, so the strongest empirical case remains the less rigorously specified human evaluation.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful problem: open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation can suffer from noisy multi-view object captions caused by occlusion and poor viewpoints, and improving node/edge reliability is relevant for robotics and embodied AI.

The proposed pipeline is coherent at a high level, combining dynamic point-cloud downsampling, re-shot view selection, uncertainty estimation, and context-based caption refinement. The manuscript is generally understandable and includes implementation details such as backbone choices, thresholds, and prompts for key VLM/LLM calls.
The reported human-evaluated node and edge precision improvements over ConceptGraphs are large, and the ablations suggest that re-shot uncertainty estimation is the most important component.
The paper considers both accuracy and efficiency, and the dynamic downsampling idea is simple and potentially useful for reducing object mapping cost.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is too limited for the strength of the claims. Evaluation is only on Replica indoor scenes, with no real-world RGB-D sequences, no cross-dataset validation, and no demonstration on downstream robotics tasks despite motivating the work through safety-critical robot use.

The human evaluation protocol is underspecified. The paper does not report number of annotators, number of evaluated nodes/edges, inter-annotator agreement, exact sampling protocol, or statistical uncertainty. Since the headline gains rely heavily on human judgments, this is a major weakness.

The semantic segmentation and ablation evaluations use GPT-4o as a semantic assigner for predicted captions, introducing a black-box and potentially biased evaluator. This also makes comparisons to prior methods difficult to interpret and may partially reward outputs phrased in ways favorable to the same family of models used in generation.

The novelty is incremental. Much of the pipeline follows ConceptGraphs, while the additions are relatively heuristic: rendering a best-view point cloud image, filtering captions by CLIP text similarity, nearest-object retrieval, and prompt-based refinement. The paper does not provide deeper theoretical justification or a rigorous uncertainty model.

The efficiency claim is narrow. The reported speedup appears to cover only object mapping time, not the full pipeline including re-shot rendering, repeated VLM calls, RAG refinement, and LLM edge generation. This is especially problematic because open-vocabulary 3DSG methods are often dominated by foundation-model inference cost.

Several methodological details are unclear or inconsistent. The paper calls retrieval semantic-aware, but the described retriever is position-based nearest-object retrieval. The dynamic voxel-size formula has questionable units and can increase point density for small objects, yet the paper broadly frames it as an efficiency improvement without sufficiently analyzing memory/runtime tradeoffs across object scales.

The baselines are incomplete for ECCV standards. The paper compares mainly to ConceptGraphs variants for scene graph quality and reports other methods only for segmentation from prior papers. It does not convincingly compare against recent open-vocabulary 3D scene graph or mapping systems under a unified protocol.

Reproducibility remains weak despite a reproducibility statement. Important prompts and non-critical hyperparameters are deferred to future code release, and no code is currently provided. The use of proprietary GPT-4/GPT-4o models also limits reproducibility and makes results sensitive to API/model changes.

The edge generation contribution is particularly thin: expanding relation labels and adding few-shot examples is a prompt-engineering modification, and the evaluation does not deeply analyze relation types, failure modes, graph connectivity quality, or whether the additional valid edges are actually useful.

The writing and presentation contain many grammatical issues and formatting problems, and some claims are overstated, such as being the first to address aggregation noise or presenting a heuristic caption-agreement score as uncertainty without sufficient validation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practical limitation of open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation: noisy multi-view object captions caused by occlusion and poor viewpoints. The proposed re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is well motivated and directly targets this failure mode.

RAG-3DSG is a coherent system contribution: dynamic downsample-mapping, best-view point-cloud re-rendering, uncertainty-based caption filtering, object-level retrieval context, and expanded edge prompting fit together naturally within the ConceptGraphs-style pipeline.

The empirical results on Replica are encouraging. Human evaluation reports clear gains over ConceptGraphs and ConceptGraphs-Detector in node precision (0.82 vs. 0.68/0.58) and edge precision (0.91 vs. 0.82/0.85), while also reducing duplicate objects and preserving more valid nodes/edges.

The ablations are useful and support the core design choices. Removing re-shot estimation, RAG, or concatenated re-shot prompts degrades performance, with the strongest drop for removing re-shot guidance, which strengthens the causal case for the main component.
The dynamic downsample-mapping strategy is simple but practical, and the reported mapping speedup is valuable for a pipeline whose open-vocabulary components are already expensive.
The manuscript is generally clear, with understandable motivation, equations, pipeline diagrams, implementation details, appendix examples, and an explicit reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The evaluation scope is narrow. Experiments are limited to Replica indoor scenes, with no evidence on real sensor data, ScanNet/3RScan/HM3D-style datasets, outdoor or cluttered environments, or downstream robotic tasks. This limits confidence in the claimed robustness and practical impact.

The human evaluation protocol is underspecified. The paper does not report the number of annotators, sample counts, inter-annotator agreement, statistical significance, or whether annotators were blind to method identity. Since the main 3DSG gains depend on human judgments, these missing details matter.

The semantic segmentation results are mixed: the method is essentially tied with ConceptGraphs on mAcc and slightly worse on f-mIoU, and substantially below OpenMask3D on f-mIoU. This is not fatal because segmentation is not the main contribution, but it weakens the broader claim of improved mapping quality.

Runtime evidence is incomplete. The paper reports a strong speedup for object mapping, but not full end-to-end runtime including SAM, GPT-4o-mini captioning, GPT-4 prompting, re-shot rendering, retrieval, and edge generation. The method may remain expensive because it relies heavily on proprietary foundation models.

The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The method mostly composes established ingredients: ConceptGraphs-style mapping, CLIP/SAM/VLM captioning, best-view rendering, uncertainty filtering, and retrieval augmentation. The integration is useful, but the algorithmic advance is incremental.

The RAG component is fairly simple: retrieval uses nearest object position and only a single nearby low-uncertainty caption as context. More semantic or graph-aware retrieval baselines would make the RAG claim more convincing.

The ablation evaluation uses GPT-4o as a semantic assigner, which may introduce opacity and potential bias. More transparent automatic metrics, human validation of assignments, or sensitivity analysis would improve trustworthiness.

Edge evaluation reports precision but not recall or graph-level coverage. Since the method generates more valid edges than baselines, precision alone does not fully characterize graph quality or possible missing/extra relationships.

strengths: The paper addresses a real weakness of open-vocabulary 3D scene graph pipelines: noisy multi-view aggregation under occlusion and limited viewpoints. The diagnose-then-rectify framing is sensible, and using active re-shot views to estimate object-level semantic uncertainty is a useful contribution for 3DSG construction.

The method is evaluated on multiple 3D scene graph benchmarks, includes comparisons to relevant open-vocabulary baselines, and reports both node and edge metrics. The ablation study supports the importance of re-shot verification, RAG retrieval, and concatenated re-shot/crop prompting.

The human evaluation on Replica is a valuable complement to automatic open-vocabulary metrics, with a stated annotation protocol and inter-annotator agreement. The reported gains in node precision, duplicate reduction, and edge precision suggest the approach can produce cleaner scene graphs.
The paper is generally clear in motivation and pipeline structure. Figures communicate the core idea well, and the method is positioned appropriately against passive frame-selection approaches.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The work combines known components: SAM/CLIP object fusion, VLM captioning, point-cloud rendering from selected viewpoints, nearest-neighbor contextual retrieval, and LLM relation generation. The paper would be stronger if it more sharply separated what is algorithmically new from engineering composition.

Several technical details needed for reproducibility are underspecified or deferred to supplementary material: the caption clustering procedure, reliability thresholding, exact prompts, rendering settings, retrieval document construction, relation prompting, and hyperparameter sensitivity. These details materially affect performance in VLM/RAG systems.

The main automatic gains are sometimes modest and uneven. On edge prediction, Ours-GPT is only slightly better or tied with OpenFunGraph on several metrics, and Ours-LLaVA is worse than OpenFunGraph for some edge scores. Some strong claims such as “hallucination-free,” “readiness for reliable real-world deployment,” and “exceptional resilience” are overstated relative to the evidence.

The evaluation may not fully isolate the proposed contributions from foundation-model choice. GPT-4o variants are compared with prior systems that may not use the same model capacity or prompting budget, and the paper relies on GPT-4o as a semantic assigner in Replica evaluation, which raises concerns about model-induced bias.
The human evaluation compares mainly against ConceptGraphs/ConceptGraphs-Detector, not the strongest OpenFunGraph baseline, limiting the strength of the fine-grained semantic-quality claim.

The real-world robot deployment is mostly qualitative. It demonstrates feasibility, but does not provide task-level success rates, quantitative localization-noise analysis, runtime on the robot, or failure cases, so it should not be used as strong evidence of deployment readiness.

The re-shot assumption can fail when point clouds are incomplete, textureless, merged across instances, or geometrically distorted. The paper discusses noise stress tests, but the injected pose noise is narrow and may not capture common segmentation, depth, texture, and reconstruction failures.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem for open-vocabulary 3D scene graph construction: semantic inconsistency from occlusion, constrained viewpoints, and noisy multi-view aggregation. This is a real limitation for robotics-oriented 3DSG systems.

The proposed pipeline is intuitively motivated: use reconstructed geometry to render an additional object view, estimate caption consistency, and use more reliable nearby objects as context for uncertain object caption refinement.

The manuscript includes comparisons on SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D, a human evaluation on Replica, ablations, and a small real-robot deployment demonstration, which gives the work broader experimental coverage than a purely synthetic evaluation.

Some empirical results are directionally positive, especially the ablation showing that removing the re-shot component causes a large drop on Replica and the human evaluation reporting better node precision than ConceptGraphs variants.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest. The method is largely a composition of existing components: SAM/CLIP object mapping, VLM captioning, simple viewpoint scoring, nearest-neighbor contextual retrieval, and LLM edge labeling. The paper frames this as a major active-verification/RAG contribution, but the algorithmic core is fairly heuristic and incremental.

The main benchmark gains are small and not consistently compelling. On SceneFun3D, Ours-GPT improves object R@10 over OpenFunGraph by only 2.4 points and edge R@10 by 1.7 points, while edge R@5 is worse than OpenFunGraph. On FunGraph3D, edge R@10 is tied with OpenFunGraph and edge R@5 improves by only 0.6. These margins do not support the paper’s strong claims of decisive or hallucination-free improvement.

The comparison is potentially unfair or at least insufficiently controlled. Ours-GPT uses GPT-4o, while many baselines use different or weaker model choices; Ours-LLaVA is more comparable but often has smaller gains and sometimes worse edge metrics than OpenFunGraph. The paper does not isolate how much improvement comes from stronger VLM/LLM backbones versus the proposed re-shot/RAG mechanism.

The uncertainty estimation is conceptually circular: the re-shot caption is treated as an active verification signal, but it is also generated by a VLM and may itself be wrong, especially when the point cloud is incomplete or texture-poor. The paper does not evaluate calibration of the uncertainty score, failure cases, or whether low uncertainty actually predicts correctness.

The robustness claims are overstated. The “extreme” noisy pose test uses only 2 cm translation and 1 degree rotation noise, and the method concatenates the re-shot with the best original crop, so the experiment does not convincingly demonstrate that the re-shot mechanism itself is robust to degraded reconstruction. The real-robot deployment is qualitative and anecdotal, with no quantitative success rates, latency, or comparison.

The human evaluation is useful but limited. It compares only against ConceptGraphs variants, not the strongest OpenFunGraph baseline, and reports precision/valid-count/duplicates without a fully normalized metric that accounts for over- or under-prediction. Details of scene sampling, annotation interface, and exact units are limited.

The edge generation contribution is weak. The method mostly follows ConceptGraphs with an expanded relation set and prompting, while reported edge gains are marginal. Since edge performance depends heavily on LLM prompting and BERT-similarity matching, the evidence does not establish a robust advance in relationship reasoning.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the main paper. Important prompt templates, parameter analyses, runtime details, and likely implementation choices are deferred to supplementary material. The method depends on proprietary GPT-4o for the best results and includes API cost estimates, but lacks enough detail to reproduce all evaluation decisions confidently.

The writing repeatedly overclaims, using phrases such as “hallucination-free,” “readiness for reliable real-world deployment,” and “exceptional resilience” that are not justified by the evidence. This weakens confidence in the scientific case.

There are presentation and clarity issues, including awkward equations/text extraction artifacts, undefined or under-specified clustering of captions, unclear thresholding for uncertainty, and limited discussion of limitations or failure modes.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation: noisy cross-view aggregation under occlusion and poor viewpoints. The proposed diagnose-then-rectify framing is well motivated for robotics settings where semantic errors can cascade into unsafe behavior.

The core technical idea is appealing: use geometry-based virtual re-shots to estimate object-caption uncertainty, then use low-uncertainty objects as semantic anchors for object-level retrieval-augmented refinement. This is a sensible and original combination of active viewpoint reasoning and 3DSG construction.

The experimental evidence is broad for an Algorithms/General submission: two real-world benchmarks, a Replica human evaluation, ablations, pose-noise stress tests, runtime discussion, and a physical robot deployment. The human evaluation is especially useful because open-vocabulary scene graph quality is difficult to capture with automatic metrics alone.

Results are consistently strong. The method improves object recall over OpenFunGraph on both SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D, and the Replica human study shows substantially better node precision, edge precision, and fewer duplicate objects than ConceptGraphs variants.

The ablation study supports the main design claims: removing re-shot uncertainty causes the largest degradation, while removing RAG, using random retrieval, or dropping concatenated re-shot/crop prompts all reduce performance.
weaknesses: Some important implementation details are deferred to the supplementary material, including prompt templates, exhaustive parameter analyses, and runtime profiling. For a method whose behavior depends strongly on VLM/LLM prompting, retrieval choices, and thresholds, this weakens reproducibility from the main paper alone.

The method relies heavily on large vision-language models, and the strongest results use GPT-4o. The LLaVA variant helps, but the paper could better separate gains due to the proposed pipeline from gains due to model capacity, prompting, or proprietary model behavior.

Edge prediction improvements are comparatively modest in the main benchmark table, especially on FunGraph3D where Ours-GPT ties OpenFunGraph at R@10 and only slightly improves R@5. Since the title and claims concern 3D scene graphs, stronger relationship-specific analysis would make the case more convincing.

The real-world robot deployment is mostly qualitative. It demonstrates feasibility, but there is no quantitative task success, latency-throughput measurement during deployment, or comparison against baselines on the robot platform.

Several design choices appear heuristic, including the top-50% split between low- and high-uncertainty objects, the view-score weights, nearest-object retrieval, and the relation category set. The ablations validate components broadly but do not fully test sensitivity to these choices.

The paper claims hallucination-free or near hallucination-free graphs in places, but the evidence supports reduction rather than elimination of hallucinations. This wording should be softened to better match the reported precision values.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph construction: noisy multi-view aggregation under occlusion and constrained viewpoints. The diagnose-then-rectify framing is well motivated for robotics settings where semantic errors can cascade into poor downstream decisions.

The proposed combination of virtual object re-shots, consistency-based uncertainty estimation, and object-level retrieval anchors is technically plausible and clearly described at a high level. The re-shot scoring terms and uncertainty-guided RAG are intuitive, and the ablations generally support the importance of the re-shot, concatenation, retrieval, and uncertainty-gating components.

The experimental scope is broader than many papers in this area: results are reported on SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D, with additional Replica human evaluation, noisy-pose stress tests, hyperparameter studies, runtime discussion, and a physical robot deployment. The human evaluation includes a stated annotation protocol and inter-annotator agreement.

The method improves object recall over strong open-vocabulary baselines, including OpenFunGraph, and the analysis convincingly argues that better node semantics can improve downstream edge prediction. The LLaVA variant is useful because it shows the approach is not exclusively tied to a closed commercial VLM.
weaknesses: The contribution is somewhat incremental in algorithmic terms: it is a pipeline-level combination of known ingredients, including SAM/CLIP mapping, point-cloud rendering from candidate viewpoints, VLM captioning, LLM aggregation, and nearest-neighbor RAG. The paper’s novelty is in the integration and uncertainty use, but the technical depth of the new components is moderate.

The evaluation has several fairness and reproducibility concerns. The strongest variant relies on GPT-4o, and the ablation/evaluation on Replica uses GPT-4o as a semantic assigner, which risks evaluator-method coupling. The paper does not clearly specify code/model release, exact API settings, random seeds, or full prompts/few-shot examples, and some prompt demonstrations are explicitly omitted.

The edge-prediction gains are not uniformly strong. On FunGraph3D, Ours-GPT matches OpenFunGraph at Edge R@10 and only slightly improves Edge R@5, while Ours-LLaVA is below OpenFunGraph on edge metrics. This weakens the claim of a broadly superior 3DSG generator, especially because edge quality is central to scene graphs.

The human and robot evaluations are useful but limited. Replica human evaluation compares mainly against ConceptGraphs variants rather than the strongest OpenFunGraph baseline, covers only 8 scenes, and uses synthetic/clean geometry. The real-world robot trial is offline, appears small and only partially quantified, and reports node precision against one baseline without detailed scene count, object count, or statistical variation.

The method’s dependence on reconstructed object geometry is only partially addressed. The noisy-pose test is helpful, but virtual re-shots can fail for sparse, transparent, reflective, thin, deformable, or heavily incomplete objects; the paper gives a case study of failure recovery but lacks a systematic failure analysis or limitations section.

Several design choices appear heuristic and dataset-sensitive, including top-50% low-uncertainty anchors, KMeans with K=3, one nearest retrieved object, fixed re-shot weights, and the eight-relation edge taxonomy. Ablations help, but they are mostly on Replica and do not fully establish robustness across domains or relation vocabularies.

The paper overstates some claims, such as readiness for reliable real-world deployment and exceptional resilience, given that the system is offline, foundation-model dependent, and evaluated in a limited physical setting. A more calibrated discussion of computational, privacy/API, and safety limitations would strengthen the submission.

strengths: The paper targets a real problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph construction: noisy cross-view aggregation under occlusion and limited viewpoints. The idea of using rendered object re-shots to diagnose semantic inconsistency is intuitive and relevant to robotics-oriented 3DSG pipelines.

The manuscript is generally well organized and includes multiple forms of evidence: comparisons on SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D, human evaluation on Replica, component ablations, hyperparameter studies, runtime discussion, and a physical robot demonstration.

The ablations suggest that the proposed ingredients are not entirely cosmetic: removing re-shot guidance, RAG, concatenated views, or uncertainty filtering degrades performance, with the re-shot component appearing especially important.
The authors provide useful implementation details such as prompts, core hyperparameters, dynamic downsampling intuition, and some runtime/cost estimates.
weaknesses: The main contribution is less convincing than claimed. Much of the pipeline is a combination of existing SAM/CLIP/VLM/LLM components, view rendering heuristics, nearest-neighbor contextual prompting, and ConceptGraphs-like edge generation. The paper frames this as a major active-verification/RAG advance, but the algorithmic novelty appears modest for an Algorithms/General ECCV submission.

The evaluation is not strong enough to support the very broad claims of robustness, state-of-the-art performance, and real-world readiness. SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D contain only 20 and 24 scenes, Replica human evaluation uses 8 scenes, and the robot evaluation is described with limited detail, no clear sample size/statistical analysis, and mostly qualitative evidence.

The comparisons raise fairness concerns. The strongest variant uses GPT-4o, while baselines may not benefit from the same model capacity or prompting effort. Table 1 also includes a Passive VLM (gpt-5.2) setting without clear methodological explanation or citation, which makes the experimental story harder to trust.

Several metrics are fragile for open-vocabulary 3DSG. Predicate evaluation relies on BERT embedding similarity, Replica semantic evaluation uses GPT-4o as a semantic assigner, and human judging is limited. These choices may favor fluent captioning/prompting rather than genuinely correct 3D scene graph construction.

The technical soundness of the uncertainty estimate is questionable. Reliability is defined through CLIP text similarity between a re-shot caption and passive crop captions, but if the re-shot is wrong, incomplete, textureless, or biased by point-cloud artifacts, the mechanism can confidently propagate errors. The paper shows one recovery case but does not systematically quantify such failure modes.

The RAG module is quite weakly justified: retrieving only the nearest low-uncertainty object assumes local spatial context is semantically helpful, but this can easily inject misleading context. The paper reports that top-3/top-5 retrieval hurts, which suggests the retrieval formulation is brittle rather than broadly robust.

The real-world deployment claims are overstated. The system is offline, depends on remote high-performance compute and/or proprietary API calls, and the robot experiment does not demonstrate closed-loop downstream task success despite repeatedly motivating safety-critical robotics use.

Reproducibility remains limited. Some few-shot demonstrations are omitted, exact VLM settings and prompts are only partially specified, proprietary models are central to the best results, and code/data release is not discussed. This makes it difficult to verify whether gains come from the proposed method rather than prompt/model choices.

The writing is polished but often promotional, with phrases such as 'firmly proves', 'exceptional resilience', and 'readiness for reliable real-world deployment' exceeding what the evidence establishes. A more restrained claim would be easier to credit.

strengths: The paper addresses an important failure mode in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation: noisy multi-view aggregation under occlusion and poor viewpoints. The proposed diagnose-then-rectify framing is well motivated for robotics settings where incorrect object semantics can cascade into bad downstream decisions.

The active re-shot guided uncertainty estimate is a sensible and fairly original contribution for this problem. Rendering an object-centric best view from reconstructed geometry, then comparing it with passive crop captions, gives a practical way to identify ambiguous nodes rather than blindly aggregating all observations.

The object-level RAG module is simple but effective: low-uncertainty objects become contextual anchors for rectifying high-uncertainty nodes. The paper gives clear intuition, case studies, and ablations showing that re-shot verification, concatenated visual prompts, and uncertainty-guided retrieval are complementary.

The empirical evidence is broad. The method is evaluated on SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D, with additional human evaluation on Replica, robustness tests under injected pose noise, hyperparameter studies, runtime discussion, and a real-robot deployment. The reported node improvements over OpenFunGraph are meaningful, including 90.2 R@10 on SceneFun3D and 83.0 R@10 on FunGraph3D for the GPT variant.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and the supplement improves reproducibility by including pseudo-code, prompts, hyperparameter sweeps, and deployment details.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate rather than transformative. The system combines known components, including SAM/CLIP, VLM captioning, LLM aggregation, heuristic view scoring, and retrieval-augmented prompting. The main insight is valuable, but the algorithmic machinery is mostly a careful composition of existing tools.

The edge-generation claim is somewhat overstated. Edge gains are modest and not uniformly dominant: for example, OpenFunGraph has higher SceneFun3D Edge R@5 than Ours-GPT, and FunGraph3D Edge R@10 is tied. The paper itself suggests that much of the edge improvement comes from better node captions rather than a substantially improved relation model.

The evaluation depends heavily on large proprietary or rapidly changing VLMs. GPT-4o is central to the best results, and Table 1 even includes a Passive VLM with gpt-5.2, which raises reproducibility and comparability questions. The LLaVA variant helps, but the strongest claims still rely on closed models and prompt behavior.

The “open-vocabulary” framing is slightly weakened by constraining relations to a small fixed taxonomy of support, containment, part-whole, proximity, and none. This is reasonable for stable evaluation, but the paper should be more careful about what is open-vocabulary: primarily object/node semantics rather than full graph semantics.

The real-world robotic deployment is encouraging but limited. The system is offline, uses remote GPU processing, and the real-robot quantitative evaluation appears to be on a small custom indoor dataset with only a ConceptGraphs comparison. This supports feasibility, but not yet broad deployment readiness.

Some reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the useful supplement. Several few-shot prompt demonstrations are omitted, API settings and model versions are not fully pinned, and no release plan is described. For a prompt-sensitive pipeline, these details matter.
